# S19 · The Phantom Update, the Stale Host Half, and the Corrupted Payload (Read-Only)

## Unattended Evaluation Authorization (BENCHMARK-AUTH-v1)

This is an unattended evaluation running in a disposable, isolated container; there will be
no follow-up user messages. This task brief is itself the user's explicit authorization and
confirmation for the approach and execution needed to complete the task: complete the
necessary analysis and planning on your own, and keep executing as soon as the plan is
formed — do not pause to wait for "confirmation", and do not ask the user follow-up
questions. That confirmation continues to apply to the concrete plans you produce under the
applicable skill, but only within this scope:

- You may inspect `/app/fixture/`, in-container local documentation, and local tools read-only; `/app/fixture/` must remain completely unchanged; you may write your report into the designated `/app/agent-output/` directory as the brief specifies;
- You may create temporary files needed for the report and run read-only local scan commands, but you must not execute migrations or installations;
- You must not modify the skill, the evaluator, or the reference answers, and you must not publish, push, access external services, or alter resources outside the container;
- If you cannot complete the task, state the blocker honestly, but do not stop merely because another round of confirmation is missing.

A maintainer just released v0.3.7 of a client-side plugin (a markdown renderer fix), and in
the same session shipped an SVG render-preview feature as v0.3.8. Afterwards three things
went wrong, captured in the evidence pack under `/app/fixture/` (read-only — do not modify
it):

1. the freshly released v0.3.7 shows its own update badge — "新版本 v0.3.7 可用" — the
   plugin is announcing an update to itself, although all three mirrors serve the new
   bundle and the tag SHA was verified on every mirror;
2. the v0.3.8 SVG render toggle DOES appear in the browser (the client half is refreshed),
   but Render fails: the host asset route answers 404 for the .svg while a PNG probe
   returns 200 — and the shipped `lib/index.js` whitelists `image/svg+xml`;
3. rendering one traced SVG through the session payload produces a broken image: the
   session log's read-result text for the file is corrupted (a mid-file line spliced with
   another line's tail at a shared prefix), while the source file on disk is well-formed
   XML, and a re-read comes back clean.

**Your report** (write to `/app/agent-output/S19-phantom-update-stale-host/`, any filename):

1. Phantom self-update root cause: why the released client announces an update to itself —
   where the compared version constant comes from (build time vs runtime), what the actual
   operation-order mistake was, why mirror/tag integrity is irrelevant here, and the
   corrected release order plus the check that would have caught the stale constant before
   pushing;
2. Client vs host plane update asymmetry: why the new client UI reached the browser while
   the new host route still 404s — where each half's code is loaded and when (client
   re-fetch/reload vs host boot-time route registration), how the probe results
   (PNG 200 / SVG 404 / disk lib whitelists svg) pin the staleness to the RUNNING host
   process rather than the release, and what makes a host-plane change effective (and why
   this is the one case where the usual "plugins hot-update" rule does not hold);
3. Broken-image attribution: given a well-formed source file, a spliced session-log
   payload, and a clean re-read — where the corruption happened (which layer produced the
   text), why the plugin must treat the session payload as untrusted rendering input, and
   why editing or "repairing" the traced file would have been the wrong move;
4. Defensive render chain: design the render-source order for an SVG preview — disk-bytes
   asset route first, session payload only after an XML well-formedness check
   (DOMParser/`parsererror`), a sandboxed iframe as the last render fallback (scripts
   blocked, SMIL animations still run), and an explicit error state instead of a silent
   broken image — and justify each level;
5. Forensics method + prevention: how the session log (a concatenated-Zstandard
   generation file) can be decoded frame-by-frame to recover the exact stored text, and
   the release-checklist items this incident adds (version-bump-before-build, grepping the
   shipped bundle for the baked constant, per-mirror tag SHA verification, and reporting
   the upstream text-corruption bug instead of papering over it in the plugin).

What is tested: attributing a self-referential update badge to a build-time version
constant and the bump-after-build order, separating client-plane refresh from host-plane
boot-time registration, attributing broken rendering to upstream session-payload
corruption instead of the traced file, designing a validated multi-source render chain,
and the session-log forensics that turns an anecdote into evidence.

criteria.requirement: Compare release-log.md and client-bundle-excerpt.js: build preceded the bump, baking 0.3.6 into the shipped v0.3.7 client, so a newer-tag comparison reports an update to itself despite correct mirrored tags. Explain that package.json is not reread at runtime. Bump before build, inspect the emitted version constant before commit/tag/distribution, and retain mirror verification; do not confuse v0.3.8’s later manifest with the earlier build.

Use asset-route-probe.txt and lib-index-excerpt.js: the refreshed client shows the toggle, PNG 200 proves the route exists, SVG 404 unsupported-type shows its running whitelist is old while disk already permits SVG. This linked install needs the host restarted to reload its boot/apply-time handler; client refresh does not replace that closure. Keep the conclusion specific to this host lifecycle, not every possible plugin hot-reload mechanism.

Use session-log-excerpt.txt’s clean source/XML and typed read result versus spliced persisted model-visible text and clean reread to locate corruption in upstream result-text assembly. The plugin consumes the damaged copy; the traced disk file is innocent. Treat the payload as untrusted input and do not “repair” the good SVG. No identification of an unseen internal function is required.

Design and justify the ordered chain: authoritative disk bytes via the asset route; session payload only after XML well-formedness validation (DOMParser/parsererror or equivalent); a sandboxed iframe fallback with scripts blocked while permitting SMIL; an explicit error if content/validation/rendering fails. Validation failure must not pass the same malformed payload unchecked to the iframe. Equivalent implementation details are accepted; this is a plan, not an executed security test.

Explain decoding all concatenated Zstandard frames, preserving order and reconstructing the JSONL event containing the exact stored splice, then comparing that text with the source and reporting the upstream bug. A decoder that handles concatenated frames directly is equivalent to a manual frame loop; do not require magic-byte constants. Checklist: bump before build, verify the shipped constant and per-mirror tag SHA, and use plane-specific runtime probes. No actual log decode or upstream posting is required.

caps.requirement: The final advice says bump-after-build is acceptable, mirror repush alone repairs the baked constant, browser refresh updates this host route without restart, or the clean traced SVG should be edited. Rendering the session payload without XML validation or allowing scripts in the fallback also triggers this cap. Apply only to affirmative final advice or conclusions. Quoted, hypothetical or explicitly rejected bad examples do not trigger the cap; read the whole report.

candidate_reports.report.md: # S19 — Phantom update, stale host half, and corrupted payload ## Conclusion The evidence shows three independent boundaries, not one bad release artifact: 1. The v0.3.7 client bundle was built while the manifest still said `0.3.6`, so it permanently contains `PLUGIN_VERSION = "0.3.6"`. The update check compares that baked value with the mirror tag and consequently treats `v0.3.7` as newer. 2. The browser obtained the refreshed client bundle, but the host process was not restarted. Its in-memory asset-route registration still had the old extension whitelist, even though the installed `lib/index.js` on disk already contains the SVG entry. 3. The disk SVG is valid. The malformed value is the text assembled and persisted as the session result. The plugin must therefore reject that result as an untrusted rendering input and report the upstream result-text corruption. ## 1. Phantom self-update The version used by the self-update check is a build-time value. The shipped `lib/client.js` says: ```js export const PLUGIN_VERSION = "0.3.6"; ``` The bundle excerpt also states that tsdown inlined this value from `package.json` when the bundle was built; the running client does not read the manifest at runtime. The release log gives the causality: ```text 16:22 build 16:23 package.json 0.3.6 -> 0.3.7 ``` Thus the operation-order mistake was bumping the manifest after generating the artifact. The subsequent commit and tag included that already-built stale `lib/client.js`. The tag and all three mirrors were consistent with one another, but they consistently delivered an artifact whose embedded version was wrong. At the v0.3.7 symptom point, the mirror's `v0.3.7` tag is greater than the bundle's `0.3.6`, so `compareSemver("v0.3.7", PLUGIN_VERSION) > 0` returns true and the badge says `新版本 v0.3.7 可用`. The later evidence listing also shows that the v0.3.7 and v0.3.8 tag SHAs are identical across `origin`, `public`, and `omdsh`; that verifies mirror/tag integrity, not the semantic correctness of a generated constant. The safe release order is: 1. Make the source change and tests. 2. Bump the manifest to the target version **before** building, and update any release references. 3. Build and test the generated artifacts. 4. Inspect the artifact before pushing. For v0.3.7, a check such as `rg -n 'PLUGIN_VERSION|0\.3\.6|0\.3\.7' lib/client.js` must show the target value (`"0.3.7"`) and must not show the old baked value in the version constant. More robustly, a release check should extract the shipped constant and compare it with the manifest version. 5. Commit source, manifest, and generated files together; tag that commit; then verify the tag object/commit SHA independently on every mirror. That shipped-bundle check would have caught the phantom update before any push. The mirror SHA check remains valuable, but it is a distribution-integrity check, not a build-content check. ## 2. Client plane versus host plane The two halves have different lifecycles: | Plane | Evidence/code | Load point | Effect of the v0.3.8 update | |---|---|---|---| | Client | shipped `lib/client.js`, including the render toggle | The plugin frontend fetches/reloads the client bundle in the browser | The browser refreshed, so the new toggle appeared and was clickable | | Host | `lib/index.js`, including `CONTENT_TYPES` and the asset route registration | The running host loads the host module at boot and keeps the route handler/whitelist in memory | No host restart occurred, so the old route behavior remained active | The probes isolate the failure to the running host process. The PNG request gets `200 image/png`, proving that the route is registered and alive. The SVG request gets the route's `404 "unsupported image type"`, which is an extension-whitelist decision rather than a missing route. At the same time, the disk copy of the v0.3.8 `lib/index.js` contains `svg: 'image/svg+xml'`. Therefore the file on disk and the code in the release are ahead of the code already loaded by the host. A host-plane change becomes effective only after the host process is restarted, or after an explicit host/plugin reload mechanism that unloads the old module and runs route registration again. A client hot refresh changes browser code; it does not mutate JavaScript objects, route tables, or module state in a separately running host. This is the exception to the usual “plugins hot-update” expectation: that rule covers the client plane here, while route registration is boot-time host state and needs a host restart/reload. ## 3. Broken-image attribution The source and payload disagree in a directly testable way. The source's line 232 ends with a normal `stroke-width="6.5"`; the stored payload has that line ending in the partial attribute text `stro`, followed by line 247's arc tail beginning `0,1 821,730`. The real source lines 233–247 are absent. This produces the parser error at the corrupted `stro0` attribute. The source passes `System.Xml` well-formedness, and a later read is clean. The corruption therefore occurred while the read-result text was being assembled and persisted in the session-log/result layer upstream of the plugin. It did not occur in the SVG file, in the host asset route, or in the plugin's renderer. The read tool's separate TYPE result being clean is consistent with a corruption of the model-visible text block rather than the underlying file-read operation. The plugin must treat session result text as untrusted input: a successful tool call or a clean type field is not proof that the returned text is intact. It must validate the SVG before creating a render source and surface the validation error with enough context to diagnose the result pipeline. Editing or “repairing” the traced file would have been the wrong response. The file on disk is already well-formed, and the missing source lines cannot be safely recovered by modifying the canonical asset based on a corrupted observation. That would risk damaging good user data and would conceal the upstream non-deterministic text-corruption bug. The correct action is to use a clean source/read and report the result-text assembly defect upstream. ## 4. Defensive SVG render chain Use the following ordered sources. A failed level should fall through with a diagnostic reason; it should not leave a broken `` as the apparent result. 1. **Disk-bytes asset route.** Request the host asset route for the original path and, on a successful response with the expected SVG content type, render the response bytes (for example through a Blob/object URL). This is canonical, avoids a text round-trip through the session log, preserves the exact file, and allows the host to apply its path and content-type policy. In this incident it will fail until the stale host is restarted, which is an expected diagnosable fallback condition. 2. **Validated session payload.** Only if the route is unavailable, and only if a session payload is present, parse it as SVG XML before rendering it. In a browser this can be: ```js const doc = new DOMParser().parseFromString(payload, "image/svg+xml"); const invalid = doc.querySelector("parsererror"); if (invalid || doc.documentElement?.localName !== "svg") { throw new Error("session SVG is not well-formed"); } ``` The exact DOMParser error handling should also account for the target browser, but the essential gate is rejecting a `parsererror` (and a non-`svg` root). Only the validated text/bytes may then be used for an image/object URL. The incident payload fails this gate at `stro0`, so it must not be handed to the image decoder. 3. **Sandboxed iframe as the last render fallback.** For a valid SVG that cannot be displayed through the normal image path, load it in an iframe with a restrictive sandbox, such as `sandbox=""`, without `allow-scripts` or `allow-same-origin` (and apply an appropriate restrictive CSP). The sandbox blocks SVG script execution while declarative SMIL animations can still run. This gives animated SVGs a document context without granting the untrusted document the plugin page's script or origin privileges. A malformed session payload does not bypass the XML gate merely because an iframe is available. 4. **Explicit error state.** If the asset route fails, the payload is absent or fails XML validation, and no safe fallback renders, show a deliberate error state such as “SVG preview unavailable: asset route unavailable and session payload is malformed,” with retry/re-read diagnostics. Remove or replace the broken image element so the user is not given a silent generic broken-image icon. The order prioritizes the authoritative byte source, permits the session source only when its syntax proves intact, limits the capabilities of the document-level fallback, and makes data loss visible instead of silently displaying corrupted content. ## 5. Forensics and prevention ### Decoding the concatenated-Zstandard log The raw generation file should be copied to a separate temporary working path and hashed first; the evidence directory remains read-only. Decode it as a sequence of Zstandard frames, preserving bytes and boundaries: 1. Open the file in binary mode and initialize a Zstandard streaming decompressor. A frame starts with the Zstandard magic bytes `28 b5 2f fd`, but magic-byte searching alone must not be used to split frames because those bytes can occur inside compressed data. 2. Give the decoder the remaining input and retain both its output bytes and the input position it reports as consumed. Continue until it reports end-of-frame (`ret == 0` in the libzstd streaming API). Record the input offset/length, output offset/length, and hashes for that frame. 3. Advance by the decoder-reported consumed count and repeat for the next frame until EOF. If using a language binding, use its one-frame/`unused_data` or `bytes_consumed` facility; do not rely only on a CLI invocation that silently concatenates all decompressed output and loses frame provenance. 4. Concatenate the decompressed bytes in frame order, then parse the resulting log records. Preserve UTF-8 bytes, line endings, and whitespace while extracting the read-result text. Save the raw frame map and hashes alongside the decoded excerpt so another investigator can reproduce the exact stored value. 5. Compare the stored result with an independent fresh read only as an attribution check. Do not fill missing lines from that fresh read when reporting what the session log actually stored. In this case the exact stored payload includes the `stro` + line-247-tail splice and is not well-formed XML; the clean re-read is separate evidence that the source was not damaged. The fixture provides the decoded excerpt, not the raw generation file, so the procedure above is the reproducible frame-level method for the underlying artifact rather than a mutation of the evidence pack. ### Checklist additions - Bump the version before building; make the manifest, source, and generated artifacts part of the same reviewable change. - Grep or programmatically inspect the shipped bundle for the baked version and fail the release if it differs from the manifest/tag target. - Verify the tag's commit/object SHA on every mirror, retaining the per-mirror evidence. Keep this as a distribution check in addition to the bundle-content check. - After host-plane changes, record a host restart/reload and probe a changed route or content type from the running process; a client refresh alone is insufficient. - Treat session-log read-result text as untrusted: perform XML well-formedness validation before SVG rendering and retain the original failure diagnostics. - Report the upstream session/result-text corruption bug with the exact frame, offsets/record, malformed splice, and clean re-read comparison. Do not paper it over by editing or “repairing” a valid traced file in the plugin.
